(i) the direction of charge displacement for PL(OX)* is similar to that for other flavins in simple and complex solvents and (ii) PL(SQ)* exhibits charge displacement in the opposite direction to that of other flavins, which is consistent with the positioning of Trp382 relative to the FAD cofactor in PL(SQ).
the excited state charge distribution for PL(OX), PL(SQ), and lumiflavin are all consistent with a charge transfer state.

the direction and magnitude (i.e., vectorial charge redistribution) of charge redistribution upon photoexcitation in PL(OX) is very similar to that in simple solvents, in an FMN-binding protein and in other flavoproteins.

the Stark effect provides a powerful tool for probing the electronic structure of flavins, and that the results are of direct relevance to the mechanism of action of photolyase.
the direction and magnitude for the excited-state charge displacements in PL(SQ) is consistent with a vectorial mechanism for the electron-transfer step in PL(SQ).

the charge distribution of the two lowest energy excited states of FADH(*) is very similar in both the PL(OX) and the PL(SQ) oxidation states, and that these charge distributions are very similar to those of flavin in simple solvents.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, while the excited state of PL(OX) is similar to that of the free flavin in solution, the excited state of the semiquinones PL(SQ) is very different from that of the free semiquinone in solution.
the excited-state charge redistribution is not a simple function of the oxidation state, but rather is determined by the protein environment and the nature of the surrounding amino acid residues.

the excited-state properties of flavins in photolyases are very similar to those observed for other flavin systems, but the protein environment has been optimized for efficient vectorial charge redistribution in photoreduction.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the direction of charge displacement upon electronic excitation of the flavin cofactor in PL(OX) is not altered by the presence of the DNA substrate, but the magnitude of the charge displacement is reduced.

the direction of charge displacement is a key factor for efficient electron transfer in photoreduction of the semiquinones of photolyases and other flavin-containing photoreceptors, which is in contrast to the situation for flavin-mediated redox reactions in flavoproteins.
the direction of excited-state charge displacement can be used to predict the direction and efficiency of electron transfer between flavins and nearby residues.
